title: the WSG Dungeon Master section slice - the starting-from-scratch world-building rules from the crossroads opener and the realism-vs-fantasy Earthlike assumption through the ten map-making steps, the fault-line and hot-spot rules, the semi-finished-product political guidelines with the country example, the clustering scale-down ladder from 36 miles through 12 and 4 and 1-and-a-third to the half mile, and the winging-it improvisation rules with the cannot-uncreate law, printed pp. 103-106, CLOSING the Dungeon Master section
audit_label: R492 WSG DM section pin audit
audit_comment: The Dungeon Master section, CLOSING it. The opener: the veteran faded world and the first-timer, the crossroads, no going back without starting over. Realism vs fantasy: no uphill water, the Earthlike assumption, the familiar-features advantage, homo sapiens dominant, the world as inobtrusive backdrop, deviations on a small scale. The ten steps: the 20-to-40-mile-per-hex scale from the DMG page 47 with the 8.5-by-11 sheet covering 1600 by 1250 miles of two million square miles, the 50-or-60-mile larger scale, the pp. 124-126 hex sheets; the coastline outline and sea level; the 10,000-foot and 5,000-foot elevation lines at 5,000-foot increments; the planet placement, the five regions, the prevailing winds; the rivers high-to-sea, the Mississippi-and-Amazon rarity, the subarctic networks, the swamps in low country; the subtropical and downwind deserts; the forests near water below the tree line; the leftover hills and plains. The details: the oases and passes, the river through the desert with its non-desert banks, the fault lines at abrupt elevation and seacoasts and mountain axes, the 20-to-40-mile hot spots where magma lies close, the not-every-line-quakes latitude. The semi-finished product: the cities by water with sea outlets, the resource cities with roads, the isolation independence, the desert divide, the rivers as boundaries, the elven and dwarven enclaves, the country ABCD example. Scaling down: the seven-league-boot caveat, the eight-hex cluster three wide at one-third, the 36-12-4-1-and-a-third-half-mile ladder, the cluster maps on demand. The smaller-scale-more-detail rules with the 20-to-30-foot cliff. Winging it: the think-on-feet law, the oak-and-clearing example, the cannot-uncreate rule, the hex-paper sketching, the between-session updates, the framework closing.

consts.name: wmdHexLoMph
consts.comment: step 1, settle on a scale: the Dungeon Masters Guide page 47 recommends the scale of a world map be from 20 to 40 miles per hexagon - the low bound

consts.name: wmdHexHiMph
consts.comment: the world map scale high bound: 40 miles per hexagon per the Dungeon Masters Guide recommendation

consts.name: wmdDmgPage
consts.comment: the Dungeon Masters Guide page carrying the world map scale recommendation

consts.name: wmdPaperLongMi
consts.comment: at 40 miles per hex measured across the middle, a standard 8.5-by-11-inch piece of small-hexagon mapping paper covers roughly two million square miles - 1600 miles in the long dimension

consts.name: wmdPaperShortMi
consts.comment: the short dimension of the hex-paper coverage at 40 miles per hex: 1250 miles

consts.name: wmdPaperSqMi
consts.comment: the rough area covered by the standard sheet of hex paper at 40 miles per hex: two million square miles

consts.name: wmdBigHexLoMph
consts.comment: if the standard sheet is not large enough, fasten two or more sheets together and work in an even larger scale - 50 miles to the hex

consts.name: wmdBigHexHiMph
consts.comment: the upper larger-scale option: 60 miles to the hex; everything is scaled down later when a section needs detailing

consts.name: wmdHexSheetFirstPg
consts.comment: sheets of hex paper with different-sized hexagons are provided in the back of the book, pages 124-126 - the first page

consts.name: wmdHexSheetLastPg
consts.comment: the last of the provided hex-paper pages; the book owner may photocopy the sheets for his personal use only

consts.name: wmdPeakLineFt
consts.comment: if any peaks are higher than 10,000 feet, draw shapes around those points indicating the line of 10,000-foot elevation

consts.name: wmdMidLineFt
consts.comment: after the 10,000-foot line, do the same for a line of 5,000-foot elevation

consts.name: wmdIncrFt
consts.comment: the resulting map is a rough topographical map showing the area lines of elevation at 5,000-foot increments - the rough shape of the world in all three dimensions is determined

consts.name: wmdHotSpotLoMph
consts.comment: each hot spot is an area of 20 to 40 miles in diameter - the low bound

consts.name: wmdHotSpotHiMph
consts.comment: the hot spot diameter high bound, usually located in the lower regions of a mountain range or along a major fault line that cuts through a mountain range

consts.name: wmdClusterHexes
consts.comment: the number of smaller hexes in a cluster that one large-scale hex breaks into

consts.name: wmdClusterWideHexes
consts.comment: the cluster is three hexes wide, so the scale of each smaller hex is one-third of the world map scale - not an exact 3-to-1 ratio since the cluster hexes are always oriented differently from the larger hex, but close enough for the purpose

consts.name: wmdClusterDiv
consts.comment: the cluster scale divisor: one-third of the scale of the world map

consts.name: wmdExampleHexMph
consts.comment: the worked example: each large-scale hex is 36 miles across

consts.name: wmdFirstClusterMph
consts.comment: the 36-mile hex breaks into first-cluster hexes roughly 12 miles wide

consts.name: wmdSecondClusterMph
consts.comment: a 12-mile hex broken down gives cluster hexes 4 miles across

consts.name: wmdThirdClusterNum
consts.comment: the next step down is 1-and-a-third miles - numerator 4 over 3 (tesseract prints the garbled 1V3 miles; both reads agree on the thirds)

consts.name: wmdThirdClusterDen
consts.comment: the 1-and-a-third-mile scale denominator

consts.name: wmdHalfMileNum
consts.comment: from 1-and-a-third miles to about one-half mile, and so on - the half-mile numerator

consts.name: wmdHalfMileDen
consts.comment: the half-mile denominator; just keep going as small as the scale needs

consts.name: wmdCliffLoFt
consts.comment: a small cliff, perhaps only twenty or thirty feet high, can show up almost anywhere on otherwise flat terrain - the low bound

consts.name: wmdCliffHiFt
consts.comment: the small-cliff high bound

bools.name: wmdOldWorldFaded
bools.comment: the veteran Dungeon Master whose campaign world has outlived its usefulness: the players have explored practically every nook and cranny and his pride has waned - if the wonder and mystery is diminished for him, what must things be like for his players

bools.name: wmdFirstTimeDM
bools.comment: or the player taking the plunge to become a Dungeon Master for the first time, familiar with the rules and full of ideas aching for release

bools.name: wmdCrossroads
bools.comment: either way he stands at a crossroads, about to start a new campaign world; it all begins with the first line drawn on a blank piece of paper that will become the world map, every mark eliminating some possibilities and opening up others

bools.name: wmdNoGoingBack
bools.comment: at some point the paper begins to look like a map and there is no going back without starting all over again; by then the map must stand as a firm foundation - a structure to add detail to that can support detail without limiting creativity

bools.name: wmdNoUphillWater
bools.comment: this section will not tell you how to make a world where water flows uphill, a desert is bordered by a swamp, and a steaming tropical jungle is nestled between two arctic mountain ranges; if ideas run along those lines no help is needed - the game can be played in any kind of universe, even one where the natural laws of Earth do not apply

bools.name: wmdEarthlikeAssumption
bools.comment: the assumption underlying practically every other paragraph in the book: the campaign world is one that could exist on Earth, or at least under Earthlike conditions - water flows downhill, you cannot go from a swamp to a desert without passing through some other kind of land, and sea-level tropical terrain is not also found at high elevation among snow-covered peaks

bools.name: wmdFamiliarAdvantage
bools.comment: the first advantage of an Earthlike world: both the Dungeon Master and the players are naturally familiar with the features of the planet; say mountain and they know what it means, unlike wooden mountains which raise slippery-question, splinter-question problems that strain the players suspension of disbelief until role-playing falls away in favor of an artificial contest

bools.name: wmdHumanDominant
bools.comment: the second point: homo sapiens is the dominant and predominant creature in the game universe, and the campaign world should be one in which player characters, human or demi-human, can survive and prosper and feel at home without biological or artificial adaptation - a methane-atmosphere world gives no character in his right mind a reason to adventure for fear of breaking his life-support apparatus

bools.name: wmdBackdropRule
bools.comment: the third point: the best campaign world is everpresent but usually inobtrusive - a backdrop for the activity between the characters and creatures that live in it, the location of a conflict but not the source of the conflict itself; keep the world in its proper place by making it ordinary so the characters concentrate on what they are doing instead of where they are doing it

bools.name: wmdDeviationSmallScale
bools.comment: deviation from the norm is a good idea on a small scale: a boiling river or a forest that pulls itself underground at first frost remains intriguing when localized, but used everywhere it loses its distinctiveness and becomes an obstacle instead of an oddity

bools.name: wmdObviousOverlooked
bools.comment: the sunglasses principle: the obvious is often overlooked, and what is obvious to one person may not be apparent to another - read the step-by-step suggestions even if you know how to create a world map, in case you run across something that has not occurred to you

bools.name: wmdContinentSize
bools.comment: it is not necessary to create an entire planet at one time; stick to something the size of a continent or part of a continent

bools.name: wmdHexesRegulateOnly
bools.comment: the world outline and features need not follow the hexagon boundaries - it is much better not to so restrict yourself; the hexes are only for regulating size and distance, and it is better to draw the map in rough form on blank paper and transfer it to hex paper later

bools.name: wmdStartAtBottom
bools.comment: step 2, start at the bottom: pencil in an outline describing the coastline, planning for major islands, long peninsulas and other ultra-large-scale geographic features

bools.name: wmdLandOffEdge
bools.comment: unless there is a reason for a continent surrounded by water, extend the land mass off the edge of the map paper in at least one direction, keeping options open for connecting another land mass later or turning the continent into an island with a small extension of the original map

bools.name: wmdSeaLevelLine
bools.comment: after step 2 the map shows all the places where the land meets the sea, which by definition also shows the location of zero elevation, or sea level

bools.name: wmdPeakBalance
bools.comment: step 3, fake it to the top: place the mountain ranges and determine the tallest peaks - not too frequent or too high (characters should not scale a Mount Everest every few days), but not too low or they provide no good challenge and change of pace

bools.name: wmdPlaceOnPlanet
bools.comment: step 4, place it on the planet: decide where the world sits with respect to the poles and the equator, and note rough boundaries where the climatic zones change

bools.name: wmdFiveRegionsEnough
bools.comment: the world need not run the gamut from arctic to tropical climate, but it does not need to be hemisphere-sized to contain all five climatic regions either

bools.name: wmdPrevailingWinds
bools.comment: at this time determine the direction of the prevailing winds in each climatic area, using the weather-generation system in the appendix for general rules to aid the decisions

bools.name: wmdRiversHighToSea
bools.comment: step 5, just add water: rivers begin at high elevation and run toward the ocean or some other place at or near zero elevation; a large river usually has several tributaries flowing into it

bools.name: wmdRareRiverSystems
bools.comment: extremely large river systems such as the Mississippi or the Amazon, with all the tributaries that feed them, are rarely found more than once or twice in a continent-sized area

bools.name: wmdSubarcticWater
bools.comment: large inland bodies of water are somewhat less frequent in subarctic climates than in warmer areas, but a subarctic region may be laced with a dense intricate network of smaller rivers and lakes - Canada is the example, with Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake contradicting the frequency statement

bools.name: wmdDontStreamEveryHex
bools.comment: do not be bashful about laying in rivers and lakes, but do not run a stream through every hex unless designing a world with no deserts

bools.name: wmdSwampPlacement
bools.comment: step 5 is also the time to decide where the swamps go: in areas of low elevation, usually near or on the seacoast and usually in an area with a lot of rivers or lakes

bools.name: wmdDesertSubtropical
bools.comment: step 6, what is for desert: on Earth most deserts are located in subtropical climate and the part of the temperate zone closer to the subtropical area - the southern half of the zone in the northern hemisphere, the northern half in the southern hemisphere

bools.name: wmdDesertWinds
bools.comment: the desert location is because of global wind patterns: prevailing winds blow generally east to west around the equator and usually in the opposite direction in the temperate regions; where they meet in the upper atmosphere over the area in between, the cool upper air descends, gets warmer, retains more moisture, and the water vapor stays suspended instead of falling as precipitation

bools.name: wmdDesertDownwind
bools.comment: farther from the tropics deserts are often located on the downwind side of high mountain ranges: the air rises and cools against the slope, releasing precipitation on the wind-facing side, and by the time it crosses over all or most of its moisture is depleted

bools.name: wmdDesertObliterateRiver
bools.comment: with those two facts in mind place the deserts, and be prepared to obliterate a river or at least change its course if the map shows water flowing through an area that would make a good desert - have an eraser handy

bools.name: wmdForestPlacement
bools.comment: step 7, may the forest be with you: mark off the forest areas, remembering they are more likely along or near large bodies of water

bools.name: wmdForestLimits
bools.comment: do not go above the tree line where arctic climate begins, and do not put a forest right next to a desert unless creating a region of unearthly terrain there for a specific reason

bools.name: wmdHillsOrPlains
bools.comment: step 8, none of the above: any terrain not designated seacoast, mountains, swamp, desert or forest must be either hills or plains

bools.name: wmdAdjacentToMountainsHills
bools.comment: if an area has no other distinguishing characteristics, the area adjacent to a mountainous region should be considered hills; spot some hilly regions in the middle of flat featureless areas just for variety, and as the next-to-last step anything else is plains

bools.name: wmdLargeScaleDetails
bools.comment: step 9, large-scale details: narrow the scope a bit - does the huge desert have an oasis or more than one, is there a pass through that awesome mountain range; mark these now so they do not have to be added when characters decide to look for them

bools.name: wmdRiverThroughDesert
bools.comment: large-scale additions and alterations: a thin strip of forest on either side of the big river slicing a vast plain is fine, and a river coursing through a desert is okay but must be bordered by a couple of strips of something other than desert - keep making finishing touches until satisfied with the lay of the land

bools.name: wmdPointsOfInterest
bools.comment: step 10, points of interest: pinpoint the locations of special isolated features resembling the Grand Canyon, Death Valley or the Yellowstone area, and determine if the world has earthquakes or volcanoes and where the fault lines and hot spots go

bools.name: wmdQuakeFaultLines
bools.comment: an earthquake can occur almost anywhere, but the most frequent and most severe quakes take place along major fault lines, often located where the land rises abruptly in elevation and especially near the seacoast - the San Andreas Fault in California is the example - or in the middle of a mountain range running along the long axis of the chain

bools.name: wmdHotSpotDefinition
bools.comment: individual volcanoes do not need to be placed on a very-large-scale map any more than every individual mountain peak does, but the hot spots must be known: the areas where volcanoes will be found, where magma lies close to the surface

bools.name: wmdNotEveryLineQuakes
bools.comment: not every major fault line produces frequent earthquakes and not every hot spot contains active volcanoes, so do not be stingy about locating these special features - the characters have no way of knowing they exist until they become active, and a long-dormant volcano springing to life by design beats doing it on a whim

bools.name: wmdMoreDecisionsBetter
bools.comment: the more decisions made in the creation stage, the fewer times you will find yourself caught short later

bools.name: wmdBringItAlive
bools.comment: the map is a one-of-a-kind creation but still not ready for adventures until it is brought alive: divide the terrain into countries, sketch the political boundaries and decide where the major population centers are - a much more complex and difficult process than that sentence indicates

bools.name: wmdCitiesByWater
bools.comment: guideline 1: the largest population centers are usually located adjacent to large bodies of water, especially along the seacoast or on the shores of bodies of water with an outlet to the sea - the health of a city depends on commerce, and the most efficient way to move trade goods is by boat or ship

bools.name: wmdResourceCities
bools.comment: guideline 2: other large cities may be located in areas with an abundance of a useful natural resource - a city can spring up in the foothills several days travel from the nearest large river, as long as a road exists or can be built to a city on the river, with miners bringing their take to be assayed, refined and sold to a caravan that transports it to the manufacturing and shipping center

bools.name: wmdIsolationIndependent
bools.comment: guideline 3: areas that are physically isolated tend to be politically independent, at least at the beginning of the world political history - an area ringed by or composed entirely of high mountains has a different government than the areas around it, Switzerland being the modern-day example

bools.name: wmdDesertDivides
bools.comment: the areas on either side of a vast desert will usually not belong to the same country, since a single central government cannot successfully exercise its power across a large expanse of impassable terrain

bools.name: wmdRiversBoundaries
bools.comment: guideline 4: in the absence of other factors, rivers often serve as political boundaries, to the advantage of the adjacent countries since there can be no doubt about where one country ends and another begins

bools.name: wmdEnclavesSuited
bools.comment: guideline 5: enclaves of humanoids and demi-humans usually occur in terrain suited to them - elves tend to be more numerous in forests, dwarves in mountains, and so forth

bools.name: wmdFleshOutWorld
bools.comment: flesh out the world in large scale by spotting the larger cities and the places where a creature type forms the predominant resident population, outline the countries perhaps leaving some political boundaries indefinite - that is how wars get started

bools.name: wmdCountryExample
bools.comment: the worked example: Country A dislikes Country B for sending refined iron ore eastward to Country C across an almost-impassable mountain range; B sells the ore for weapons sent to the mountain passes near its border with A; Country D watches from the south playing a waiting game while building its military strength - three short paragraphs producing a simple situation with a wide range of consequences and several opportunities for adventurers to defuse or aggravate the tension

bools.name: wmdAdventurersSurvive
bools.comment: no matter which government the party works for, the characters are going to spend a lot of time in the wide open spaces and must know how to survive on the way to accomplishing what they are being paid to do

bools.name: wmdWorldMapNotDaily
bools.comment: unless every character wears seven-league boots the world map is not useful in day-to-day adventuring: even at the smallest recommended scale there will be times when characters traveling overland do not cover the span of a single hex in a single day

bools.name: wmdClusterMethod
bools.comment: a good way to scale down is clustering: break a single large-scale hex into a cluster of eight smaller hexes and make a more detailed map of the area the large hex covers

bools.name: wmdClusterOnDemand
bools.comment: small-scale maps are not needed for every hex on the world map, at least not all at once: concentrate on the area the characters are in and heading toward, and be prepared with cluster maps of the territory the party is expected to travel through, drawn in as much detail as necessary

bools.name: wmdUnexpectedDirection
bools.comment: if the characters head in an unexpected direction, either call a brief halt and generate some rough small-scale maps, or simply improvise without interrupting the flow of play

bools.name: wmdGeneralityMap
bools.comment: the large-scale world map is a collection of generalities: the big green spot is a forest hundreds or thousands of square miles in area but not all forest; the large grassy plain is not just flat terrain - the map is a picture of the world as viewed from hundreds of miles overhead, where small-scale variations are not visible but are nevertheless there

bools.name: wmdTerrainVaries
bools.comment: as each hex breaks into a cluster keep in mind that terrain usually does not stay the same on a mile-by-mile basis: the monotony of a flat grassland is often broken by a grove of trees several hundred yards wide or a small forest a mile or two in diameter; a slight dip in a forest elevation makes swampy ground among the trees

bools.name: wmdMoreDetailEachStep
bools.comment: with each step to a smaller scale the detail of the hex maps and the variety in terrain and special features should increase: if a river cuts through the hex being scaled down, draw in streams coming off the main branch; if the large-scale hex takes in part of a lake, sketch in swampy ground along the lakeshore at the next smaller scale - a swamp that does not show up on the large-scale map but is there nevertheless

bools.name: wmdThinkOnFeet
bools.comment: a Dungeon Master must be able to think on his feet: no matter how much planning goes in, the players will occasionally have their characters do something or go somewhere unanticipated - more often than not the problem is an opportunity in disguise, the opportunity to create and decide on the spot during the game

bools.name: wmdImproviseWithinReason
bools.comment: when characters move into an area not yet mapped in detail, improvise and invent within reason any special features that make the segment more interesting or give the players things to think about - more than just there is forest around you as far as you can see

bools.name: wmdOakExample
bools.comment: the worked improvisation: a lightly wooded area where most trees are the same height except one big oak to the east towering over the others, a clearing to the north where sunlight reaches the ground, the land sloping gradually upward to the west with few trees at the peak

bools.name: wmdImprovisationPays
bools.comment: improvising this way impresses the players with the Dungeon Master organization and attention to detail, and more importantly creates possibilities for excitement and intrigue: climb the oak and maybe see something important in the distance, move to the clearing and maybe find a path through the rest of the forest, climb the slope and maybe discover a sharp dropoff with a small pool at the bottom

bools.name: wmdCantUncreate
bools.comment: the only rule when improvising: you cannot un-create something later - keep track of what you tell the players, either in brief notes or preferably by sketching the features just described on a handy sheet of hex paper

bools.name: wmdRepeatVisits
bools.comment: if the characters visit a spot more than once they will expect to see the same details described when they first arrived; between sessions take a few minutes to update the collection of small-scale maps incorporating the features devised during the game, so you will not be caught short if the characters backtrack or stumble upon the same location later

bools.name: wmdFrameworkClosing
bools.comment: the closing: all the rules still provide nothing more than a framework upon which the world and adventures are built - the pieces to a puzzle with an infinite number of different solutions, and it is up to the Dungeon Master to put those pieces together

examples.note: the recommended hex scale range is strictly ordered, 20 up to 40, as is the larger 50-to-60 option
the standard-sheet coverage arithmetic: 1600 miles by 1250 miles is the two-million-square-mile area, and the larger-scale floor sits above the recommended ceiling
examples.expr: m['wmdPaperLongMi']() * m['wmdPaperShortMi']() != m['wmdPaperSqMi']() or m['wmdBigHexLoMph']() <= m['wmdHexHiMph']()

examples.note: the topography: the 10,000-foot peak line is twice the 5,000-foot mid line, and the contours step at the 5,000-foot increment
the hot spot diameter range matches the recommended hex scale range exactly, 20 to 40 miles
the cluster: eight smaller hexes in a cluster three hexes wide, at one-third scale
examples.expr: m['wmdClusterHexes']() != 8 or m['wmdClusterWideHexes']() != 3 or m['wmdClusterDiv']() != m['wmdClusterWideHexes']()

examples.note: the cluster ladder: 36 miles over the divisor 3 gives the 12-mile first cluster, 12 over 3 gives the 4-mile second, and 4 thirds gives the 1-and-a-third third step
examples.expr: m['wmdExampleHexMph']() != m['wmdFirstClusterMph']() * m['wmdClusterDiv']() or m['wmdFirstClusterMph']() != m['wmdSecondClusterMph']() * m['wmdClusterDiv']() or m['wmdThirdClusterNum']() * m['wmdClusterDiv']() != m['wmdSecondClusterMph']() * m['wmdThirdClusterDen']() or m['wmdThirdClusterNum']() * m['wmdHalfMileDen']() <= m['wmdHalfMileNum']() * m['wmdThirdClusterDen']()

examples.note: the half-mile floor of the scale ladder is exactly one over two
the hex-paper sheets run from page 124 through 126 in order
the small cliff range runs 20 to 30 feet, strictly ordered
the Dungeon Masters Guide scale recommendation cited from page 47
